title: Transaction Utility (The Joy Of A Good Deal)
description: We get two separate pleasures from a purchase: the actual value of the item (acquisition utility) and the feeling of getting a bargain compared to a reference price (transaction utility). We often overpay for the thrill of the deal.
shortDescription: We get two separate pleasures from a purchase: the actual value of the item (acquisition utility) and the feeling of getting a bargain compared to a reference price (transaction utility). We often overpay for the thrill of the deal.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We get two separate pleasures from a purchase: the actual value of the item (acquisition utility) and the feeling of getting a bargain compared to a reference price (transaction utility). We often overpay for the thrill of the deal.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A jacket originally $200, on sale for $80, feels better than an identical jacket priced at $80 with no sale tag.
You buy something you don’t need because the discount is “too good to pass up.”
Black Friday frenzy: people fight over TVs not because they need them, but because the perceived deal is euphoric.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Checking the “original” price to feel good about the purchase.
Bragging about how much you saved, not how much you spent.
Buying extra items to hit a free‑shipping threshold, “saving” money you wouldn’t have spent otherwise.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “It would have been stupid not to buy it at that price.”
“I saved so much money.” (while spending money you didn’t plan to)

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re more excited about the discount than the product.
You buy things solely because they’re on sale, and they gather dust later.
You compare the sale price to an inflated “original” price, which may be fake.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Richard Thaler identified transaction utility as a separate component of overall utility. The feeling of getting a deal activates reward centers in the brain, sometimes more than the item itself.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Ask: “Would I buy this if it were just priced at this amount, without any ‘original’ price?”
Ignore the “was” price; evaluate the item at its current cost relative to your needs and budget.
When you feel a rush from a discount, pause for an hour. The high fades, and you can decide clearly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming all discounts are real. Sellers often inflate reference prices to manufacture transaction utility.
Thinking that “saving” money on a purchase is the same as keeping money. Not spending $100 on a $200 jacket still means you spent $100.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A shopper sees a handbag marked down from $500 to $150. She buys it immediately, thrilled by the $350 “saving.” She never uses the bag and later realizes she needed that $150 for a repair. The transaction utility tricked her into valuing the deal over the dollars.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: A discount is not a deposit into your bank account. The deal high fades; the purchase stays.
